title: Plasma-cut the overhanging strip off an installed skid's deck plate along a hand-held straightedge
instruction: Cut the overhanging strip off the skid's deck plate along the white line with the plasma torch, guiding the torch along the straightedge, then put the torch and the straightedge back where they were and move both hands away.
context: Workers in nuclear cleanup and scrap yards cut up steel equipment where it stands, often with a hand torch. The Department of Energy carries $538.6 billion of federal environmental liabilities (Treasury FY2025). Plasma arc cutting was the primary method of segmenting reactor internals at Shoreham and Yankee (EPRI 1003029) and is routine for size reduction in decommissioning (Anderson et al. 2026, testing 3 mm glovebox-type plate). At Rocky Flats, workers in protective clothing cut up gloveboxes with plasma torches (DOE); Sellafield's first glovebox, in 2024, was cut by hand in air-fed suits, and robotic dismantling gave under a fifth of the manual dose in a study cited there. Scrap is cut apart with gas or plasma torches by hand (OSHA 3348), with no general robotic method (IEEE CASE 2021). The cutter's manual directs a straightedge guide for straight cuts. Here the plate is an installed skid's deck, with its cabinet and junction box in place.
setup: Positions in cm, x forward from the arm bases' midpoint, y toward the left arm. A skid stands on the table: two 2 x 2 x 1/4 in steel angles (outer faces at y -8.5 and y 18.5, x 21.5 to 35.5) carry a 3 mm mild-steel deck 53.8 mm above the table, from y -15.6 to 18.5. A white line at y -10 runs the deck's full 14 cm from its far edge (x 35.5) to its near edge (x 21.5); the 55 mm strip right of it (0.18 kg) overhangs the right angle. A 4-11/16 in square steel junction box, 2-1/8 in deep, is mounted on the deck at (28.5, 11.95). The skid's control cabinet (12 x 42 x 25 cm) stands with its face at x 45.5, 10 cm past the deck's far end. A steel dross pan (x 19.5 to 38.5, y -19 to -8.7, 1.2 cm rim) is on the table under the overhang. The plasma torch (0.10 kg at the hand; a balancer carries the lead) lies on its rest centred at (25, -25): a 19 cm handle along y with a yellow grip block on top, and at its +y end a vertical head ending in a 2 cm copper drag shield, 5.9 cm from the grip block. A loose aluminium straightedge (1 x 1/4 in 6061 flat bar, 18 cm, 0.14 kg) lies flat on the deck from x 20.5 to 38.5 with its working edge at y -9 (one shield radius from the line) and a red 3 cm handle block 11.5 cm behind the edge. Both grippers start open at the ready pose. Real trial: a Powermax30 AIR on 120 V at 20 A, deflector on, shield dragged on the deck; the supervisor holds a hold-to-run switch wired in place of the trigger and closes it only by the arc-on rule below; one emergency stop; shade 5 filters on the cameras, welding screens and blanket, sand in the pan, fan, extinguisher and fire watch (README).
scoring: The 14 cm line is 14 segments of 10 mm. Arc on: the torch in a hand (tool point within 45 mm of the handle centre), within 30 degrees of square, the shield's rim from 1 mm into the deck's top to 2 mm above it, over the deck between its ends and within 10 mm of the line; each step adds 0.05 s to the segment under the nozzle. A segment is sound when cut through (0.482 s or more of arc: 20.75 mm/s or slower, the cutter's maximum for 3 mm at 20 A), not overheated (1.575 s or less: half the rated 12.7 mm/s, a modelling choice), the nozzle never more than 2 mm from the line and the torch never more than 10 degrees from square over it, and for 80% or more of its arc time the shield's side within 1 mm of the straightedge's working edge with the straightedge flat on the deck (1 mm, 3 degrees). The strip drops only when all 14 are cut through. Score 0 if the torch or straightedge falls off the table or the other hand comes within 45 mm of the nozzle with the arc on. Otherwise 0.8 x the share of sound segments (rounded to 0.001; 7 of 14 sound scores 0.4); 0.9 with all 14 sound and the strip in the pan (centre 25 mm or more below its start, over the pan); 1.0 with, as well, the torch back on its rest (15 mm in plan, 6 mm in height, tilted under 10 degrees, turned under 20), the straightedge still where it was laid (handle block within 20 mm in plan and 6 mm in height, tilted under 3 degrees, turned under 20), both grippers 6 cm or more from the torch, straightedge and strip, and those still at the end. Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: cut edge 18 to 22 mm from a witness line, a 0.5 mm feeler against a straightedge on the edge, engineer's square on the face, dross and top corner checked, read under 50 C (README).
reset_notes: Simulation: the strip is put back on its weld at reset. Real trial, each time: fit a new 3 mm deck plate on the skid with the line and witness line scribed; empty the strip and dross from the pan with tongs once under 50 C and level the sand; lay the torch on its rest and the straightedge along the line; check the nozzle and electrode and wipe spatter off the deflector and the straightedge's edge.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with real contact: the shield slides on the deck and bears on the loose straightedge, which moves unless the hand presses it. The arc, kerf, heat and dross are not simulated: cutting is arc time per 10 mm segment from the torch's pose, and the strip hangs on one weld released when the last segment is cut through. No sparks, fume, lead drag or warping; cameras unfiltered; no sand in the pan.
